results.title: Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs
results.author: Anton Smith
highlights:
Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs

Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs

Preemptible VMs now come with dynamic spot pricing: more flexible access to capacity, better control of costs.

September 22, 2026

A virtualized compute environment creates opportunities for both cloud providers and their customers. One is preemptible VMs (PVMs): interruptible compute for non-critical workloads that runs on pre-allocated, temporarily idle capacity. For the GPU compute market, which is still dealing with a scarcity problem, this distribution model presents an elegant solution. Today, we’re introducing dynamic spot pricing for PVMs: an algorithm that reads available capacity and real-time demand signals from Nebius users to set the price automatically.

...

The spot pricing system aggregates information about existing capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers, then calculates a spot price for preemptible VMs on a specific GPU type in a specific region. The spot price changes over time and cannot fall below a set price floor. There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Note

Update, November 2, 2026: this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.

...

To see the current spot price, customers can simply create a compute instance and select a preemptible virtual machine. The price is currently updated up to every 15 minutes and is the same for every resource type that runs on preemptible capacity, including Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

...

You can start using preemptible VMs today, and the new tooling and settings are already available. Dynamic pricing itself takes effect on 8 October. If you already use preemptible resources, you’ll need to configure a price setting for them before that date. Look out for an email with more information.

results.title: Neocloud vs Data Center: Rent GPUs or Own & Colocate? | Enzu
highlights:
Neocloud vs data center is a rent-or-own decision, and for GPUs that stay busy it usually goes to owning. In our worked example, 64 B300s owned in colocation cost about $4.71 per GPU-hour over three years, against $9.50 on-demand at Nebius from October 1, 2026 and about $6.18 at its best published reserved discount. For short or bursty work, rent.

On October 1, 2026, Nebius, one of only two GPU clouds rated Platinum in SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX 3.0, raises its on-demand B300 price from $7.85 to $9.50 per GPU-hour. If you rent, that kind of repricing is part of what you're buying.

results.title: Nebius Introduces Dynamic Spot Pricing for GPU VMs as AI Compute Demand Tightens | AI Industry Today
results.author: AI Industry Today Desk
highlights:
Nebius is turning unused GPU capacity into a real-time compute market. From October 8, preemptible VM prices will adjust by GPU type and region as often as every 15 minutes based on available supply and customer demand, with users able either to cap the price they are willing to pay or follow the market to maximize availability. Coming just after Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates amid strong AI demand, the move shows neocloud pricing splitting into premium guaranteed capacity and dynamically priced interruptible compute — making when and where an AI workload runs an increasingly important part of compute economics.

 AI Industry Today Desk Published Sep 23, 2026 · 12:25 UTC 

 Nebius logo and wordmark displayed against a dark blue data center background with illuminated server racks and cloud imagery. 

Nebius is introducing dynamic spot pricing for its preemptible virtual machines, replacing fixed discounts with market-based GPU prices that respond to real-time capacity and customer demand. Nebius said the new pricing system will take effect on October 8 and will calculate a separate spot price for each GPU type and region, giving AI developers more flexibility to trade off compute availability against cost.

Until now, Nebius priced preemptible VMs by applying discounts set by the company to its standard on-demand rates. Under the new system, an algorithm will aggregate available capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers and update the spot price as frequently as every 15 minutes. Prices will remain between a predefined floor and ceiling, with the ceiling set one cent below the corresponding on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Customers will be able to choose between two pricing strategies. Users focused on minimizing cost can set a maximum price per GPU-hour for a specific accelerator and region. If the spot price is at or below that threshold, the workload runs at the prevailing market price. If the price rises above the user’s limit, the preemptible instance stops while its data is retained and can be restarted once pricing falls back within the specified range.

Alternatively, customers can follow the market price without setting a cap, prioritizing continued access to capacity over the lowest possible cost. In that mode, users pay the dynamic spot price and generally retain their preemptible VM unless Nebius reclaims the underlying capacity or carries out maintenance. Kubernetes can automatically restart interrupted preemptible instances, while standalone VMs can be restarted manually or through Terraform, SDKs, APIs or command-line tools.

Nebius will also publish up to 30 days of spot-price history, allowing customers to identify periods of lower demand and schedule flexible workloads accordingly. The same spot price will apply across Nebius services that use preemptible capacity, including virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

...

The change comes as AI compute remains unusually tight. Reuters reported last week that Nebius will raise on-demand prices for selected Nvidia GPUs by 17% to 21% from October 1, its second increase in three months. The company cited surging demand for infrastructure used to train and run AI models, while also raising prices on some CPU and memory resources.

Current Nebius pricing shows how large the gap between interruptible and guaranteed capacity can be. Before the dynamic system takes effect, Nebius lists preemptible B200 capacity at $3.95 per GPU-hour versus $7.15 on demand, H200 at $2.45 versus $4.50, and H100 at $2.15 versus $3.85. Those fixed preemptible rates will be replaced by the new demand-sensitive mechanism from October 8.

...

- Nebius on X — Spot Pricing Announcement(Official social announcement confirming that pricing will vary by GPU type, region, capacity and demand)

results.title: GPU rents rise 17–21% on 1 October while the neoclouds' own loan documents show borrowing 100bp dearer
highlights:
The pricing half of the thesis is verifiable at source, which is the most useful thing here. Nebius's own pricing page carries two columns — current, and effective 1 October 2026 — showing on-demand per-GPU-hour rates going from $3.85 to $4.50 for H100, $4.50 to $5.40 for H200, $7.15 to $8.50 for B200 and $7.85 to $9.50 for B300. Those are increases of 16.9%, 20.0%, 18.9% and 21.0%. Roundups describing this as up to 21% are accurate; the table is better, because it says which chip and from what. It is a rate card, not a revenue disclosure — what Nebius intends to charge, not what it will collect.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Jump 22% in a Month as GPU Shortage Hits Firms and Labs - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: An Hye-ji, Intern Reporter
highlights: - Key summary: Vessl AI, a domestic neocloud company, raised the hourly rate for Nvidia H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39 on the 1st of this month, a 24.7% increase. The price adjustment marks the start of similar moves in Korea after U.S. neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius successively raised GPU rental rates. Vessl AI procures most of its roughly 7,000 GPUs through leasing. According to Ornn, an AI computing trading platform, the hourly cloud rental rate for the H100 rose 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, reaching about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. The impact is spreading to industry and research, with some companies abandoning bids for government-led AI transformation projects because they could not secure GPUs, while universities and research institutes scale back the size of their research.

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

results.author: Abhi Asok
highlights:
Quick answer

Nebius is the best GPU cloud provider for most AI teams in September 2026. It holds SemiAnalysis's top Platinum reliability rating, publishes per-GPU on-demand prices (H100 $3.85 per GPU-hour, rising to $4.50 on 1 October 2026) and offers the newest Blackwell GPUs. Pick RunPod for the cheapest easy H100s ($2.69 Community Cloud, $3.49 Secure Cloud), CoreWeave for large training clusters, Lambda for simple on-demand instances, and Modal for serverless GPUs billed by the second.

...

### Nebius

by Nebius · Usage-based · $3.85/GPU-hour (H100, on-demand; $4.50 from 1 Oct 2026)

8.4/10

Nebius is the provider we would pick for most serious AI work in 2026. In September 2026 SemiAnalysis moved it up to Platinum in ClusterMAX 3.0, the top tier, shared only with CoreWeave. SemiAnalysis describes it as strong in every category and able to charge a premium for that quality.

Unlike many cluster specialists, Nebius publishes simple per-GPU prices. An H100 costs $3.85 per GPU-hour on demand today, an H200 $4.50 and a B200 $7.15. Preemptible capacity, which can be taken back when others need it, starts at just $0.79, and multi-month reservations cut up to 35%.

The catch is timing. Nebius has announced a price rise from 1 October 2026: H100 goes to $4.50 and B200 to $8.50. At the new rate it is still cheaper than every hyperscaler, but no longer the bargain it was. Egress on its standard object storage also costs $0.015 per GiB.
